lessons.title: Third down
lessons.objective: You can say why third down decides drives.

payload.prompt: Why is third down so important to both offense and defense?

options.text: It is usually the last real chance to keep the drive going before a punt or kick
The offense always throws on third down
The defense cannot blitz on third down

explanation.correct: Exactly. Third down is the make-or-break moment. Convert and the drive continues. Miss and the offense usually punts or kicks.
explanation.incorrect: Third down decides the drive. Convert and keep going. Stall and the team usually has to hand the ball over or kick.

payload.prompt: Second and eight, gain only three. What's the result?

options.label: New set of downs
options.consequence: Three yards is short of the eight you needed, so there is no new set of downs yet.
considerations: A new set of downs comes only when the ball reaches the first-down line.

options.label: Third and five coming
options.consequence: After gaining three, it becomes third and five. You still need five more yards to keep the drive alive.
considerations: Down stays the same (third), yardage to gain decreases by the amount you gained.

payload.expertNote: Down and distance math is simple: yards gained reduce the yardage needed, and you only reset to first down when you reach the line to gain.

payload.prompt: On third and long, the defense can call any coverage knowing the offense probably needs to throw. True or false?

scene.alt: A defense stacking coverage players deep on third and long yardage, preventing deep completions.

explanation.correct: True. Third and long is usually a passing down, so the defense can drop extra defenders into coverage and send its best pass rushers.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. When the marker is far away the offense usually has to throw, so defenses play for the pass.

payload.prompt: Match each third-down yardage to the call the defense might make.

pairs.definition: Defense stacks the box to stop a sneak or short run; the offense could go for it.
A balanced call, could be run or pass; defense watches for play-action.
Passing down; defense plays tight coverage on receivers and may not worry about the run.

explanation.summary: Third down yardage tells both teams a lot: short means sneak or run, medium could go either way, long usually means a pass.
explanation.sayThisLine: Third and short: stuff the box. Third and long: guard the receiver.

payload.prompt: A team with a great third-down conversion rate is usually which?

options.text: Good offensively; they move the ball and keep drives alive
Losing a lot because their offense is on the field too much
Bad at defense because third down happens all the time

explanation.correct: Converting third down is an offensive skill. High third-down conversion rate means your offense extends drives and scores.
explanation.incorrect: Third-down efficiency is an offensive stat. Convert third downs and your offense gets more chances to score.

payload.prompt: Order these third downs from shortest to longest.

items.text: Third and one: sneak or dive
items.why: One yard is the shortest, often a quarterback sneak.

items.text: Third and four: power run or quick pass
items.why: Four yards is a medium-short gap.

items.text: Third and eight: a pass with some depth
items.why: Eight yards usually means a throw past the line to gain.

items.text: Third and twelve: deep route or screen
items.why: Twelve yards is the longest, a true passing down.

explanation.correct: The longer the distance, the more the offense has to throw. One yard can be a sneak, twelve usually means a pass.
explanation.incorrect: Put the yardage in order from one yard up to twelve. Short yardage favors the run, and long yardage favors the pass.

lessons.title: Go for it?
lessons.objective: You can weigh a fourth-down decision the way fans do.

payload.prompt: Fourth and two at the 35. Down four, two minutes. Go?

options.label: Go for it
options.consequence: Aggressive but modern. Convert and you're near the goal. Fail and give the ball away.
considerations: Down 4 with time running out requires a touchdown.
A field goal would leave you down one, so you would still need a touchdown.
Fourth and two is a good bet to convert.

options.label: Kick field goal
options.consequence: A field goal makes it one point down, so you still need a touchdown, and the defense gets the ball back.
considerations: Safer, but it still leaves you behind.
It uses precious time.

options.label: Punt
options.consequence: Gives the other team possession when you need to score. Wastes time.
considerations: Punting surrenders the ball late in the game.

payload.expertNote: Late-game math changes everything. A field goal does not win the game, so you need a touchdown anyway, and going for it on fourth and short is a sound choice.

payload.prompt: About how often do NFL offenses convert on fourth and two?

explanation.correct: A little over half the time. That is high enough that many coaches now go for it in the right spots.
explanation.incorrect: NFL teams convert fourth and two a little more than half the time. That is why analysts say going for it is often worth it.

payload.prompt: Which is NOT a factor in a fourth-down decision?

options.text: The score and time left
The color of your jerseys
Field position and the opponent's strength

explanation.correct: Jersey colors do not matter in fourth-down math. Score, time, field position, and matchups do.
explanation.incorrect: Fourth-down decisions depend on the game situation and your team's ability on fourth and short, not what they are wearing.

payload.prompt: Modern analytics say coaches should go for it on fourth and short early in the game, not just at the end. True or false?

scene.alt: A coach pointing to analytics sheets showing fourth-down win probability.

explanation.correct: True. Analytics models often favor going for it on fourth and short, even early, depending on field position and how good the team is at converting.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Modern coaches use data to go for it earlier in games, not just when desperate.

payload.prompt: Match each situation to the call.

pairs.definition: Often go for it; a touchdown is worth far more than a short field goal.
Usually punt; a failed try hands them a short field.
Go for it; a field goal would not be enough.

explanation.summary: Field position and game situation decide fourth-down calls. Short yardage near the goal line and late in a trailing game favor going for it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Goal line: often go. Deep in your own end: punt. Trailing late: aggressive.

payload.prompt: The old saying was always punt on fourth down except at the goal line. Why has that changed?

options.text: Coaches are younger and more aggressive
Data shows going for it on fourth and one or two improves win probability
The rules changed and fourth down is easier now

explanation.correct: Analytics and math changed the game. Going for it on fourth and short wins more games than punting.
explanation.incorrect: The rules stayed the same, but the math is new. Win probability favors aggressive fourth-down calls.

lessons.title: The red zone
lessons.objective: You can explain why scoring gets harder near the goal line.

payload.prompt: Why is it harder to score once the ball reaches the red zone?

options.text: The field is shorter, so routes are compressed and defenders can play tighter coverage
The defense is allowed to use more players
The quarterback has less time to throw

explanation.correct: The red zone is tight. Receivers have less room to separate, and the end zone is only ten yards deep, so deep shots become tougher.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone (inside the 20) compresses every route. You can not throw deep balls and receivers can not separate easily in that space.

payload.prompt: Tap the red zone on this field.

diagram.alt: A football field showing yard lines from the offense's perspective, with the opponent's end zone at the top and the 20-yard line marked.

explanation.correct: The red zone is the area inside the opponent's 20-yard line. Inside it, the end zone is close and the space is cramped.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone is inside the opponent's 20. Field goals get easier, but touchdowns get tougher because there is no room.

payload.prompt: Red-zone drives sometimes end in a field goal instead of a touchdown. True or false?

scene.alt: An offense in the red zone settling for a field goal instead of pushing for a touchdown.

explanation.correct: True. With so little room, defenses tighten up, and offenses often settle for three points.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Inside the 20 the defense has less field to cover, so stalled drives often end in field goals.

payload.prompt: At the opponent's 15 with three downs. Which plan?

options.label: Mix runs with quick passes
options.consequence: The defense cannot sit on one thing, and short throws and runs both work in tight space.
considerations: The red zone compresses routes and coverage
A mix keeps the defense guessing
Three tries allows both

options.label: Run every down
options.consequence: Runs gain reliable yards, but the defense can load up once it knows what is coming.
considerations: Runs are dependable in short space
The defense stacks up if it is predictable

options.label: Throw long every down
options.consequence: There is almost no deep space to throw into, and covered receivers make this a risky throw.
considerations: The end zone is only ten yards deep
Receivers have little room to separate

payload.expertNote: Space is tight in the red zone, so offenses lean on short passes, runs and misdirection. There is no single best call, but doing the same thing every down is predictable.

payload.prompt: Match each zone to what it means for scoring.

pairs.definition: Inside the opponent's 20-yard line; where every yard matters and defenses tighten up.
The front edge of the end zone. The ball crossing it for a touchdown is worth six.
Roughly inside the opponent's 35 for a strong kicker; a closer kick is a safer three points.

explanation.summary: The closer to the end zone, the harder it gets to move the ball but the bigger the payoff.
explanation.sayThisLine: Red zone: tight space. Goal line: the end zone edge. Field goal range: a kick is realistic.

payload.prompt: In the red zone, the defense has the advantage because?

options.text: Less field to defend; coverage is tighter and receivers have nowhere to hide
The offense is not allowed to use running backs
The defense gets an extra player for red zone plays

explanation.correct: The red zone is small, so defenses have less ground to cover. Receivers find it harder to get separation and plays are compressed.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone compresses everything. Every route is tighter and separation is harder, which helps the defense.

lessons.title: Kick or go for two
lessons.objective: You can explain when a team goes for two.

payload.prompt: Down 8 before your touchdown. Kick for one or go for two?

options.label: Kick for one
options.consequence: After the touchdown you are down 2. The kick makes it 1, so you still need another score.
considerations: A kick leaves you down 1
You would need another score
You give up the chance to tie right away

options.label: Go for two
options.consequence: After the touchdown you are down 2. A successful two-point try ties the game.
considerations: Success ties the game
A conversion works about half the time
If it fails you are down 2 and need a score anyway

payload.expertNote: Two-point math: go for it when it changes the score more than a kick does. Down 2 after the touchdown, one point still leaves you behind, so two to tie makes sense.

payload.prompt: Going for two is always a fifty-fifty gamble and never a good idea early in the game. True or false?

scene.alt: A short-yardage play from the two-yard line where the offense attempts a two-point conversion.

explanation.correct: False. Two-point tries work about half the time, which is worth roughly the same as a kick on average. So they are a real option, especially when the score makes one point matter less than two.
explanation.incorrect: Not always. Two-point conversions succeed about half the time, close to the value of a kick, so they can be good math.

payload.prompt: Which situation favors going for two?

options.text: You lead by 16 late in the fourth quarter
You trail by 2 after a late touchdown, before the try
You lead by 14 in the first quarter

explanation.correct: Trailing by 2 after the touchdown, a good try ties the game. A kick only makes it a one-point deficit.
explanation.incorrect: Going for two helps when it changes the result of the game, like tying it. Big leads or early games rarely call for it.

payload.prompt: Complete this about two-point decisions.
payload.template: Trailing by {{score}} after a touchdown, a kick leaves you {{result}}. A successful two-point try ties it.

explanation.correct: Trailing by 2 after the touchdown, a kick leaves you down 1, while a made two-point try ties the game.
explanation.incorrect: Do the math: down 2, a kick adds one (down 1), a two-point try adds two (tied).

payload.prompt: Match each scoring option after a touchdown to its reward.

pairs.definition: Snap from the 15-yard line; a 33-yard kick; nearly automatic and usually safe.
Snap from the 2-yard line; run or pass; succeeds about half the time; two points if good.
Usually kick; go for two when the score makes the extra point matter, like trailing by two.

explanation.summary: Extra points are safe. Two-point tries are risky but sometimes necessary for game math.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kick it: one point, almost always. Go for two: two points, risky, only when you need it.

payload.prompt: Your touchdown cut the gap to 5 before the try. One minute left. Kick or two?

options.text: Kick; you are down 4 and need a touchdown
Go for two; if you get it a field goal ties
Kick and then try an onside kick

explanation.correct: Down 5, a kick leaves you down 4, and only a touchdown wins. A made two-pointer leaves you down 3, where a field goal ties. That is why late, down 5 is a classic go-for-two spot.
explanation.incorrect: Kick and you are down 4, needing a touchdown. Go for two and a field goal would tie. Two-point tries change what you need.

lessons.title: Two-minute drill
lessons.objective: You can describe how a team saves the clock.

payload.prompt: Order this two-minute sequence after an in-bounds catch.

items.text: Receiver catches a pass and is tackled in bounds
items.why: The clock keeps running after an in-bounds catch.

items.text: Offense hurries to the line without a huddle
items.why: There is no time to waste with the clock running.

items.text: Quarterback spikes the ball to stop the clock
items.why: A spike stops the clock at the cost of a down.

items.text: Offense runs its next play with the clock stopped
items.why: The offense can now take a breath and call a real play.

explanation.correct: The clock runs on an in-bounds catch, so the offense hurries up, spikes to stop the clock, then runs a real play.
explanation.incorrect: Start with the in-bounds catch, then the hurry-up, the spike, and finally the next real play.

payload.prompt: Snap quickly: tap with about 30 seconds left on the play clock.

explanation.correct: Quick snap. When the game clock is running, every second before the snap comes off the game clock.
explanation.incorrect: Too slow or too early. In a two-minute drill, offenses want to snap quickly while the clock runs.
explanation.sayThisLine: When the clock is running, a quick snap saves time.

payload.prompt: In the two-minute drill, why are sideline routes better than middle routes?

options.text: Sideline routes let the receiver step out of bounds to stop the clock
Sideline routes confuse the defense
Middle routes take more time to develop

explanation.correct: Sideline routes let the receiver step out of bounds, which stops the clock immediately. That saves precious seconds.
explanation.incorrect: Out of bounds stops the clock in the two-minute drill. Sideline throws set that up.

payload.prompt: At the 40, 1:00 left, down 3, one timeout. Spike or timeout?

options.label: Spike first
options.consequence: The spike stops the clock and saves your timeout, at the cost of one down.
considerations: A spike is an intentional incomplete pass.
It costs a down but not a timeout.
Use timeouts when you need to regroup.

options.label: Call timeout now
options.consequence: Wastes a timeout when the spike would do the job for free.
considerations: Timeouts are more valuable than spikes.
Save them for after plays you need to think through.

payload.expertNote: Spike first: it saves your timeout and costs only a down. You have downs to spare on first down, so the spike is the cheaper way to stop the clock.

payload.prompt: The quarterback can spike the ball on any down, including third down, to stop the clock. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback spiking the ball after an incomplete pass in the two-minute drill.

explanation.correct: True. A spike is a legal play: it is an incomplete forward pass that stops the clock and counts as a down.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the quarterback can spike the ball on any down. It is an incomplete pass that costs a down.

payload.prompt: Match each two-minute tool to what it does.

pairs.definition: A route where the receiver can step out of bounds to stop the clock instantly.
The quarterback throws the ball on the ground to stop the clock and reset; costs a down.
Stops the clock so the team can regroup; each team gets three per half.

explanation.summary: The two-minute drill is about managing every second. Sidelines, spikes and timeouts are your weapons.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sideline stops the clock. Spike stops the clock. Timeout stops the clock. Use them all.

lessons.title: Managing the clock
lessons.objective: You can spot good and bad clock management.

payload.prompt: Up 3 with the ball at midfield, 1:30 left. Run or pass?

situation.narrative: You are on offense and leading by three. The opponent has one timeout left.

options.label: Run the ball
options.consequence: A run keeps the clock moving and makes them spend timeouts.
considerations: Runs in bounds keep the clock running
Incomplete passes stop the clock
A run avoids turnovers

options.label: Throw it
options.consequence: An incomplete pass stops the clock for free, and an interception gives them the ball with time left.
considerations: Passing can stop the clock
Turnovers risk the lead

payload.expertNote: When ahead late, run the ball and keep the clock moving. Passing gives the other team free stoppages and risks a turnover.

payload.prompt: When ahead, you want the offense to use quick plays and move fast to burn the clock. True or false?

scene.alt: An offense running the ball to run down the clock while ahead in the game.

explanation.correct: False. When ahead, you want slow, methodical drives. Run the ball, take your time, use the whole play clock.
explanation.incorrect: No, when you are ahead you want to slow the pace. Run the ball and use the full 40-second play clock.

payload.prompt: When trailing late, what is the worst clock mistake?

options.text: Running up the middle so the clock keeps moving
Throwing sideline routes to get out of bounds
Taking a timeout between plays

explanation.correct: Running in bounds keeps the clock moving, which hurts a trailing team. Incompletions and sideline catches stop it.
explanation.incorrect: Trailing late, you want the clock stopped. Passes that fall incomplete or end out of bounds stop it.

statement.speaker: Broadcast analyst
statement.text: They are running the victory formation now. The game is basically over.

payload.question: What is happening?

options.text: The winning team is celebrating early
The winning team is kneeling down to run out the final seconds safely
There is a formation advantage for the ahead team
The offense is changing strategy for the last play

payload.translation: Victory formation is the kneel-down: the quarterback takes the snap and drops to a knee to waste time and avoid a costly turnover.

followUps.line: Why not run the ball for yards in victory formation?
followUps.why: Shows you know clock management: kneeling is about running time, not gaining yards.

followUps.line: Can the defense stop a victory formation play?
followUps.why: Tests your sense that kneeling is unstoppable when ahead.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask why a team would give up the chance to score more points when ahead.

payload.prompt: Match each clock situation to the right strategy.

pairs.definition: Run the ball, stay in bounds and use the full play clock.
Pass quickly, throw sidelines to stop the clock, use timeouts to regroup only when needed.
Kneel down to waste the final seconds safely without risking a fumble or turnover.

explanation.summary: Clock management depends on the score. Ahead: slow it down. Behind: speed it up. Game in hand: kneel.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ahead: run and use the clock. Behind: pass and save time. Late lead: kneel.

payload.prompt: Using a timeout to stop the clock is valuable when?

options.text: You are trailing and need to regroup to design a crucial third-down play or two-minute situation
You are ahead and want to slow the game pace
You want to stop the other team from running the clock

explanation.correct: Timeouts are best used when trailing to save time and regroup. Wasting timeouts when ahead is a clock-management mistake.
explanation.incorrect: Timeouts matter most when trailing and in a hurry. When ahead, avoid using them and let the game tick down.

lessons.title: Overtime
lessons.objective: You can explain how overtime works and who gets the ball.

payload.prompt: In NFL regular-season overtime as of 2025, what changed?

options.text: Each team gets a possession, like the playoffs
Overtime is now five minutes instead of ten
Field goals do not count in overtime

explanation.correct: Since 2025, both teams get a possession in NFL regular-season overtime, like the playoffs. A touchdown on the first drive no longer ends the game immediately.
explanation.incorrect: The 2025 rule change let both teams get the ball in overtime. It applies to regular season now too.

payload.prompt: Put the steps of NFL overtime in order.

items.text: Coin toss: the winner picks to receive or defer
items.why: The toss decides who gets the first possession.

items.text: The first team gets a possession
items.why: It can score, punt or turn it over.

items.text: The second team gets a possession to answer
items.why: Both teams get a chance to score.

items.text: If still tied, the next score wins
items.why: After both possessions it becomes sudden death.

explanation.correct: Toss, then a possession each, and if it is still tied the next score wins.
explanation.incorrect: The order is the toss, the first possession, the answering possession, and then sudden death if it is tied.

payload.prompt: You won the overtime coin toss. Receive or defer?

options.label: Take the ball
options.consequence: You set the target, and the other team knows what it needs to answer.
considerations: You control the first drive
You put the pressure on their answer
Most teams still choose this

options.label: Defer possession
options.consequence: You see their result before your drive, so you know exactly what you need.
considerations: You have the last possession
You know the target before you play

payload.expertNote: Coaches disagree about this choice. Receiving first sets the target and is still the usual pick. Deferring gives you information but not the first punch.

payload.prompt: In NFL overtime today, a first-drive touchdown ends the game at once. True or false?

scene.alt: An overtime game where one team scores and the game ends immediately.

explanation.correct: False. The other team now gets a possession to answer. After both possessions, the next score wins.
explanation.incorrect: Not anymore. Both teams get a possession, then it becomes sudden death if the game is still tied.

payload.prompt: Match each OT format to how it works.

pairs.definition: Ten-minute period; both teams get a possession, then sudden death. A tie is possible.
Fifteen-minute periods; both teams get a possession, then sudden death. Plays to a winner.
Each team starts at the opponent's 25 and they trade possessions until one team leads.

explanation.summary: NFL overtime is timed and both teams get a possession. College overtime is a shootout from the 25.
explanation.sayThisLine: NFL overtime is timed. College overtime is a shootout.

payload.prompt: What is the main benefit of having the ball second in NFL overtime?

options.text: You know the score and can plan accordingly; if they score, you can match or beat them
The defense is tired from the first possession
The second team always gets a two-point conversion

explanation.correct: You know the score before you play, so you can decide how aggressive to be. It is an information edge, not a guarantee.
explanation.incorrect: The benefit is knowing what you need before your drive. That does not make the second possession easier.
